newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul prosecutors to seek arrest of president's son.
newsitem.headline: Seoul prosecutors to seek arrest of president's son.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors grilled President Kim Young-sam's son for a second straight day on Friday and said they would seek his arrest within 24 hours.
"Prosecutors will seek a warrant to arrest Mr Kim Hyun-chul either late today or tomorrow," a prosecution official said.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said the president's second son was grilled throughout the night over kickbacks, illicit political funds and influence-peddling and the "investigation proceeded fairly smoothly".
Prosecutors said they had established the younger Kim took at least two billion won ($2.2 million) from several companies, while associates managed more than 10 billion won for him.
They said before they started questioning the junior Kim on Thursday that they had secured enough evidence to charge him with criminal offences.

The presidential Blue House on Friday braced for the arrest of the president's son. "If Kim Hyun-chul is arrested tomorrow, presidential spokesman Yoon Yeo-joon is expected to make a brief remark on the matter," a Blue House official said.
"The president himself is expected to make his stand known on the current political situation sometime next week," he added.

The Joong-Ang Ilbo daily said the arrest of Kim Hyun-chul would deal a "fatal blow" to the morality of the Kim Young-sam administration, whose image has been already tarnished by a sleaze scandal uncovered by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.
"His arrest in a way serves as a judgement on the current administration," it said in an editorial.
Eleven people, including three top aides of President Kim, stand trial for the loans-for-kickbacks scandal involving Hanbo that folded in January under five trillion won in debts.
During parliamentary hearings over the Hanbo affair, Kim Hyun-chul denied last month he took bribes from companies or meddled in state affairs.
Kim Young-sam took power on an anti-corruption platform, and his administration spent its early years flushing into the open "black" money hidden during previous corrupt governments.
Illicit slush funds helped land Kim's two immediate predecessors, Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo, in jail.
President Kim has faced mounting pressure to fully account for his campaign financing for the 1992 presidential election.
Opposition parties have alleged the president's son, who played a key role in the election, pressured banks to give loans to Hanbo as a reward for election donations of up to 90 billion won.

A survey by the Munhwa Broadcasting Corp showed a total of 52.9 percent of South Koreans polled said the president would not be able to carry out his duties properly as the head of state if he was indeed implicated in the Hanbo scandal.

But although the public clamours for answers on whether Kim Young-sam knew that key members of his anti-graft administration were on the take, only nine percent wanted his resignation or impeachment, according to the Munhwa survey.

Many civic leaders have expressed concern that a constitutional crisis, on top of an economic downturn and a string of corporate bankruptcies, may be too much for South Korea's infant democracy to bear.
Former top intelligence officer Kim Ki-sup, an associate of the president's son, is due to join Kim Hyun-chul for prosecution questioning later on Friday.

Kim Ki-sup would be questioned about a seven billion won fund the prosecution suspected he managed through an executive of the Hansol Group, the country's 16th largest business conglomerate, on behalf of Kim Hyun-chul. ($1 = 891 won)
